report.source_text: The biopsy showed infiltration by sheets of atypical plasmacytoid cells with some multinucleated forms. Skeletal muscle was also seen. There was no lung parenchyma. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that this population was positive for CD138 and MUM1 and weakly positive for CD56. TTF1, p63, S100, AE1/AE3, CD3, CD20 and CD79a were negative. Ki67 was remarkably high (90%). Further immunostains performed at King’s College Hospital reference laboratory revealed that CD38 was strongly positive, there was lambda light chain restriction seen on the immunostaining as well as ISH. Cyclin d1, CD45, pancytokeratin and kappa were negative. Epstein-Barr virus encoded small nuclear RNAs was negative.

report.source_text: Immunoglobulin studies showed a slightly low IgA level of 0.62 g/L with a normal IgM level. Protein electrophoresis demonstrated the presence of 2 g/L of paraprotein consisting of IgG lambda paraprotein and lambda light chains. Light chain studies showed a normal free kappa concentration of 6.12 mg/L and an elevated free lambda concentration of 1178.1. His kappa/lambda ratio was reduced at 0.01.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 60-year-old man presented with chest pain, back pain, abdominal distention, leg weakness, and numbness. A Chest CT scan revealed a large lobular lung mass with chest wall invasion, pleural effusion, and lumbar vertebral and pelvic bony metastatic appearances. An MRI of the spine showed widespread skeletal metastatic disease, including an intervertebral deposit causing significant thoracic cord compression. A lung biopsy confirmed plasmablastic myeloma, characterized by atypical plasmacytoid cells positive for CD138, MUM1, CD38, and lambda light chain restriction. Immunoglobulin studies further supported the diagnosis with IgG lambda paraprotein and elevated free lambda light chains. A bone marrow biopsy showed no evidence of myeloma infiltration.

key_supporting_evidence.claim: Initial presentation included chest pain, back pain, abdominal distention, leg weakness, and numbness, suggestive of widespread disease and potential spinal involvement.

Chest CT scan revealed a large lobular mass (75mm) with chest wall invasion (left 3rd rib, adjacent muscle), mild to moderate left pleural effusion, and lumbar vertebral and pelvic bony metastatic appearances.

MRI of the spine showed widespread skeletal metastatic disease, including large soft-tissue deposits in the thoracic paraspinal space and an intervertebral deposit at T4/T5 causing significant compression of the adjacent thoracic cord.
Lung biopsy pathology confirmed plasmablastic myeloma based on immunohistochemical staining (CD138+, MUM1+, CD38+, lambda light chain restriction, high Ki67; negative for other markers).
Immunoglobulin studies showed IgG lambda paraprotein (2 g/L), elevated free lambda concentration (1178.1 mg/L), normal free kappa, and a reduced kappa/lambda ratio (0.01).
Bone marrow aspirate, trephine and immunophenotyping showed no evidence of infiltration by myeloma.
